parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what the continuous light is made of on a particle picture, and what it meets inside the cool gas.
Hint 2: Remember electrons in atoms cannot take up any amount of energy - what rule controls which photons can be absorbed?
Hint 3: Consider what happens to an electron just after it absorbs a photon - where does that photon energy go next?
Hint 4: Compare the direction of the re-emitted light with the direction of the original beam to explain why some wavelengths look missing.
parts.proper_answer: Photons interact with electrons in the gas atoms. Only photons with energy equal to the difference between electron energy levels are absorbed, exciting electrons to higher levels. On de-excitation photons are re-emitted in all directions, so those wavelengths are removed from the forward beam, giving dark lines on a continuous background.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture Photons Meeting Atoms**
Think of the incident white light as a stream of photons with a continuous range of energies. Inside the cloud these photons meet electrons in the cool gas atoms. Most photons pass straight through without interacting.

Step 2: **Only Exact Energy Gaps Are Absorbed**
Electrons occupy discrete, quantised energy levels. An electron can only absorb a photon if the photon energy exactly matches a gap: $$\Delta E = E_{high} - E_{low} = hf$$ This lifts the electron to a higher level. All other photon energies cannot be absorbed.

Step 3: **Re-emission Goes In All Directions**
The excited electron is unstable and soon de-excites. The absorbed energy is re-emitted as a photon, but this happens spontaneously in a random direction - not just forwards along the beam.

Step 4: **Dark Lines In The Forward Spectrum**
So in the forward direction viewed through the grating, the continuous spectrum is missing those exact absorbed wavelengths. You see a bright continuum with narrow dark absorption lines where $$E_{photon}$$ matched an atomic transition.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: You are given $E$ for $\lambda = 420\text{ nm}$ and asked for $E$ at $740\text{ nm}$ - how does photon energy vary with wavelength?
Hint 2: Use the inverse proportion to scale the 2.96 eV value, or use $E = hc/\lambda$ with $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}$ and then convert joules to eV.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use Inverse Proportion**
For photons, $$E = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$$ so for the same $h$ and $c$, $E$ is proportional to $1/\lambda$. That means you can scale from the known value: $$E_{740} = E_{420} \times \frac{\lambda_{420}}{\lambda_{740}}$$

Step 2: **Calculate The Energy**
Insert $E_{420} = 2.96\text{ eV}$: $$E_{740} = 2.96 \times \frac{420}{740} = 1.68\text{ eV}$$ This is the same as doing $$E = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.0 \times 10^{8}}{740 \times 10^{-9}} = 2.69 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J} = 1.68\text{ eV}$$ So the incident photons span about $1.68\text{ eV}$ to $2.96\text{ eV}$.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
key_concepts: matching photon energy to level difference
hints: Hint 1: Dark lines are caused only by photons in the 1.68 eV to 2.96 eV range - look for level differences on Fig. 11.2 that lie inside this range.
Hint 2: Test differences starting from the $-3.4\text{ eV}$ level upward and see which upper levels give an energy jump that the incident light can provide.
parts.proper_answer: Draw three upward arrows all starting at $-3.4\text{ eV}$: to $-1.5\text{ eV}$ ($1.9\text{ eV}$), to $-0.85\text{ eV}$ ($2.55\text{ eV}$) and to $-0.54\text{ eV}$ ($2.86\text{ eV}$).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find Allowed Jumps In Range**
Absorbed photons must have $1.68\text{ eV} < \Delta E < 2.96\text{ eV}$. Transitions from the $-13.6\text{ eV}$ ground state need about $10\text{ eV}$ or more, so they cannot happen. Try from $-3.4\text{ eV}$: $$-3.4 \to -1.5: \Delta E = 1.9\text{ eV}$$ $$-3.4 \to -0.85: \Delta E = 2.55\text{ eV}$$ $$-3.4 \to -0.54: \Delta E = 2.86\text{ eV}$$

Step 2: **Show Them As Upward Arrows**
All three $\Delta E$ values lie inside the 1.68 eV to 2.96 eV range of the incident light, so all three can absorb and cause dark lines. On Fig. 11.2 draw three vertical upward arrows starting on the $-3.4\text{ eV}$ line and ending on the $-1.5\text{ eV}$, $-0.85\text{ eV}$ and $-0.54\text{ eV}$ lines respectively.
